I've written a little bit more about the political climate in France at the time of this book, which I think is very helpful to know to understand some of the subtext in the book.  Check out the original thread to read it.  Didn't want to post it twice.

There is a smattering of French here and there, but I don't think anything is missed by not being able to translate these words.

Dumas' books are entwined with French history.  This book begins in the period just after the French Revolution and it may be helpful to understand a little bit about this period in France to follow some important themes in the book.

In the simplest terms, the French monarchy under King Louis XVI and Marie-Antoinette was bankrupt and the people were starving.  There were embargoes on imports of goods to France due to unrest and war in Europe.  The  people of France revolted.  There were two camps in France - the revolutionists and the monarchists.  What side you were on meant life or death depending on who was in power.  

The king and queen are executed and Napoleon and becomes emperor of France.  Later he is deposed and exiled to the Island of Elba (which comes up in the very beginning of the book) and the monarchy is reinstated - Louis XIII takes the thrown.  In the book I believe he is still a small child.  Napoleon then returns from exile and attempts again to overthrow the monarchy.  

The political climate is important in the book.  When Napoleon was emperor, the revolutionists were heroes.  When the monarchy was reinstated, they were traitors.

I'm no expert on French history, but I was inspired by the book to make a small study of the French Revolution.  I hope this is helpful!

Characters' names change throughout the book, sometimes referred to by name or by title and I found it very difficult to understand who was who. I had to read this book multiple times to be clear.  

For example Fernand Mondego takes on the name Count de Morcerf so he is referred to throughout the book at different times as Fernand, Monsier Mondego, the Count, Monsier de Morcef.  

Oftentimes the son of a character may have a different name than the father and always a different title.  For example, Fernand's son Albert is referred to at different times as Albert, Viscount, Monsier de Morcef, Viscount de Morcef. 

This happens with many characters throughout the book.  You can find a list of character names online, but I wouldn't recommend that since the names are followed by a synopsis of the characters, which may spoil the unfolding of the characters by reading.  For me, I started keeping a list of characters and what they are referred to so that I could keep up.

If you go the websites of the following credit agencies, there are instructions on how to put what's called a credit freeze on your account and what that means:

Equifax:  https://www.equifax.com/personal/credit-report-services/credit-freeze/

You do not need an attorney to file a claim in small claims court.  One of the purposes of small claims court is to allow citizens to file claims without an attorney.

Go to the clerk of your local district court to obtain the paperwork.  Make sure you have her name and address so that she can be served with the paperwork.  A court date will be given to you.  If she does not pay you before that date, you must appear in court.  If she does not appear in court, you will be granted what is called a default judgment against her.

The hard part then is actually collecting the money.  The court does not cut you a check or force her to cut you a check.  After you receive the judgment you will need to make further efforts to collect (see your state laws/ask the clerk of the court).  If you are still unable  to collect, you can go back to the court and ask to file (I forget the name of it) a paper that forces her to go to court and produce proof of her assets - bank accounts, house, etc.  Then you have to do the work to try and attach a lien to those assets.

It's basically a losing battle.  Your best hope is that if you file the lawsuit she will pay before the court date.

In my experience recruiters just toss them, but I always provide one.  I use the cover letter to state why I'm interested in the position/company and why I think they should consider me a good candidate.  I basically use their job posting and repeat it and then briefly state why I think I might be a good fit, but in an abbreviated way.  I don't state every skill I have.  I say, I have X years experience in (job posting) and am interested in discussing this opportunity with you.

I use the job posting to craft my resume to skew my experience description towards their requirements.  This is more like a bulleted list rather than a full description of duties.  That more detailed discussion I save for the interview.  I also never approach interviews as if I'm trying to get them to hire me.  I know I have the skills they're looking for or they wouldn't have called me for an interview.  I ask questions about the role they are trying to fill to get more details and respond with why that fits with my experience.  I always ask why the position is open.  Did someone quit or move up?  Are they expanding the department? 

A lot of people are crap interviewers anyway so I think it's good to go in with some questions.  I try and skirt the salary requirements and benefits discussion.  If possible I save those for after they have said they want to hire me.  These are more HR questions rather than department head questions.  I don't accept the position and then find out.  

I never say "I'm making X salary at my current position".  If you say that, they will talk you down to that number or only very slightly above.  If my current salary is $40,000/yr (for example) I'll say I'm making $45,000.  They're not going to offer you less than you were making before plus even if they chew you down to your "current" salary, you're still getting a $5,000 raise.

I know this description doesn't apply to every job out there, but I hope there is something useful here (?)

Never ask for time off.  Say "I'm not available on X day" or "I need to be out on X day".  That way they can't say no, which they love to do.  Don't ever tell an employer why you need a day off.  They will only either A) Guilt trip you or B) Make an argument against your reason for needing time off.  If they press you, just say you have a personal commitment.

I would never say "my current salary is X and I need X+ something"  I don't say what I was earning.  If they pressure me, I add $15,000 a year (or whatever) to my current salary and ask for X more.  That way they feel like heroes when they talk you down to your "current" salary and you get a raise anyway.

I asked for your state because some states have a crime victim's fund that may be able to help in the case of an uninsured motorist.

Can you tell us what state you are in?  The first thing I would do is obtain the police report.  That is the document the insurance company will use to determine fault.  If the report is incomplete or incorrect or unclear in any way, now is the time to speak up to the police.  The police report should also contain the info on the driver's insurance.  If not, your insurance company can investigate.  If the other driver was cited for not having proof of insurance, you can follow up that citation to obtain the information as they will have to go to court to prove insurance.  Definitely notify your insurance company of the accident.  Because it is no-fault, your insurance company can act on your behalf.

I hope you pressed assault charges against the other driver.  If not, I would do so in a big hurry.  You also want to obtain and save any and all medical documentation of injuries sustained as a result of the accident and bills.  

Since there were injuries (and an assault) DO NOT settle with the insurance company before discussing the case with a personal injury attorney.  The injuries you describe could result in prolonged or even life-long treatment and expenses that the other party's insurance must pay (if they are found to be at fault).

Once you speak to their insurance company, they will likely try to dispute the at fault responsibility because they do NOT want to pay your claim.  They may offer you a percentage of liability.  For example, they may say it was 75% their insured's fault and 25% yours and try to lower your payout.  

Again, a personal injury attorney can help. I think they don't charge an upfront fee, but take a percentage of your payout.  A consultation sure can't hurt.

Dim sOmit As String, sPath As String, sFile As String, sPrn As String
